Research

Direct dark matter phenomenology

Non-relativistic effective field theory through to UV-complete mediator models — bridging fundamental physics and detector observables across argon, xenon, germanium and beyond.

Overview

Direct-detection experiments measure energies and rates; turning those measurements into statements about dark matter requires a theoretical framework that connects fundamental particle models to what a given detector actually sees. This is the work of dark matter phenomenology.

Our phenomenology spans non-relativistic effective field theory — a largely model-independent description of dark matter–nucleon interactions — through to UV-complete mediator models with definite high-energy completions. A recurring theme is the target dependence of signals: how the same underlying physics imprints differently on argon, xenon, germanium and other detector materials, and how combining targets sharpens what can be inferred.

Current activities

Current work includes mapping experimental sensitivity across the space of effective dark matter–nucleon operators, including interactions accessible only through forced companion operators; reinterpreting published experimental results under broader model assumptions; and cross-target comparisons that inform the design of future experiments.
